target: पूजा से मिलिए, ये मेरी सहेली हैं।
english: Meet Pooja, she is my friend.
tip: मिलना (milna = to meet) takes से (se): पूजा से मिलिए (Pooja se miliye) is literally 'meet from Pooja'. Hindi never meets a person directly – always through से (se).

target: हियरिंग एड लगाने से सुनाई देने लगा।
english: After wearing a hearing aid, he could hear.
tip: You don't just hear in Hindi – hearing comes to you: सुनाई देने लगा (sunai dene laga) is literally 'hearing began to give'. Seeing works the same way: दिखाई देना (dikhai dena).

target: घर आए मेहमान को हम चाय-नाश्ता ज़रूर पूछते हैं।
english: We always offer tea and snacks to a guest who comes home.
tip: पूछना (poochhna) usually means 'ask', but with food it means offer: चाय-नाश्ता पूछते हैं (chai-nashta poochhte hain) = we offer tea and snacks, not ask about them.

target: प्रिया ने जुगाड़ से टूटी हुई मशीन ठीक कर दी।
english: Priya fixed the broken machine through jugaad.
tip: जुगाड़ (jugaad) has no single English equivalent – a clever, improvised fix using whatever is at hand. The word covers the fix, the skill, and the mindset all at once.

target: ठगों ने राहगीरों को लूट लिया।
tip: English took 'thug' from Hindi ठग (thag) and 'loot' from लूट (loot) – both entered English in the colonial era. In this sentence they still mean robbers and robbing.

target: चाय-वाय पीकर सुषमा ने काम शुरू किया।
english: After having tea and all, Sushma started working.
tip: Hindi doubles a word with a v- echo to mean 'and such': चाय-वाय (chai-vai) = tea and whatnot. The echo वाय (vai) has no meaning of its own – it just loosens the noun.

target: कोई भी परेशानी हो तो तुरंत बताना।
english: If there is any problem, let us know immediately.
tip: बताना (bataana) here is not 'to tell' – a bare infinitive works as a gentle command for later: 'do let us know'. It is softer than the direct order बताओ (batao).

target: व्यायाम से शरीर और मन दोनों स्वस्थ रहते हैं।
english: Exercise keeps both body and mind healthy.
tip: दोनों (donon = both) follows the pair instead of leading it: शरीर और मन दोनों (sharir aur man donon) – literally 'body and mind both'. Putting it first sounds off in Hindi.

target: जयपुर को गुलाबी नगर कहते हैं।
english: Jaipur is called the Pink City.
tip: No passive 'is called' here – subjectless कहते हैं (kahte hain) means 'people call it'. जयपुर को (Jaipur ko) marks the thing being named: people call Jaipur the Pink City.

target: ज़िंदगी में उतार-चढ़ाव तो आते ही रहते हैं।
english: Life has its ups and downs.
tip: English says ups and downs; Hindi flips the order: उतार-चढ़ाव (utaar-chadhaav) is literally 'descent-climb'. Paired opposites like this behave as a single noun.

target: तिल का ताड़ बनाना बंद करो, बात छोटी थी।
english: Stop making a mountain out of a molehill; it was a small matter.
tip: तिल का ताड़ बनाना (til ka taad banaana) is literally 'turning a sesame seed into a palm tree' – Hindi's version of making a mountain out of a molehill.

target: सचिन ने दिल खोलकर सबकी मदद की।
tip: दिल खोलकर (dil kholkar) is literally 'having opened the heart'. Hindi often uses this -कर (-kar = having done) form where English wants an adverb: wholeheartedly.

target: कहने को तो बात छोटी है, पर असर बड़ा है।
english: The matter seems small to mention, but its impact is great.
tip: कहने को तो (kahne ko to) is literally 'for the saying' – it flags that what follows is only true on the surface, setting up the पर (par = but) that undercuts it.
रहा है (raha hai) = happening right now, like -ing: दुख रहा है (dukh raha hai = is hurting). Without रहा it reads as a habit, not this moment.
पौने (paune) = 'a quarter less': पौने सात (paune saat) = 6:45, quarter to seven. Hindi has one word per clock fraction – सवा (savaa = quarter past), साढ़े (saadhe = half past).
सी (si) after an adjective softens it: सुंदर सी ड्रेस (sundar si dress) = a rather pretty dress. It agrees too – सा (sa) with masculine nouns.
Adjectives not ending in -ा never change: गरम (garam = hot) stays the same with जून (June), चाय (chai = tea), पानी (pani = water). Only -ा adjectives shift.
For respect, even one person takes हैं (hain), not है. मेरे पिता हैं (my father is, respectful).
यह (yeh = this) for nearby, वह (woh = that) for far. यह मेरा भाई है = This is my brother.
मेरा (mera = my, m), मेरी (meri = my, f), मेरे (mere = my, m pl). The owned thing's gender picks the form.
तुम्हारा (tumhara = your, m). For feminine: तुम्हारी. For plural/respect: तुम्हारे.
मुझे (mujhe) = to me. With चाहिए (chahiye = want/need): मुझे पानी चाहिए = I want water. Super useful in any restaurant.
मुझे (mujhe) + X + पसंद है (pasand hai) = I like X. The thing liked stays unchanged. मुझे चाय पसंद है = I like tea.
Adjective matches the noun's gender. छोटा (chota, m) for boy/son. छोटी (choti) for girl/daughter.
क्या (kya) at the start = yes/no question. क्या आप X बोलते हैं? = Do you speak X?
Use कैसे (kaise = how) with masculine हो (ho, informal you). For respect: कैसे हैं? (kaise hain?).
कृपया (kripaya = please, formal). For favors, end with कीजिए (kijiye, polite imperative).
आइए (aaiye = come, polite imperative). For -ना verbs, drop -ना and add -इए for polite commands.
कल (kal) = yesterday OR tomorrow. Context decides. Future-leaning verb (मिलते हैं) here points forward: "tomorrow".
क्या (kya) at the start = yes/no marker OR what. Here: "what is your name?". Word order: tum-hara-naam-kya-hai.
